en: Neither from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause,
do any entities ever exist anywhere as having arisen.
There are four conditions: the causal condition, the objective condition, the immediate condition, and likewise the dominant condition; there is no fifth condition.
For the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities does not exist in conditions and so forth;
when intrinsic nature is non-existent, extrinsic nature (parabhāva) does not exist.
Action does not possess conditions, nor does action lack conditions;
conditions do not possess action, nor indeed do they possess action.
"These are called conditions because [an effect] arises in dependence upon them;
as long as [the effect] does not arise, how could these not be non-conditions? (MMK 1.5)
A condition for an object that is neither non-existent nor existent is not tenable.
Of what would there be a condition if it were non-existent, and what need is there for a condition if it were already existent?
When a phenomenon that is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent does not arise,
how can a producing cause be logically tenable under such circumstances?
This very dharma is taught as being without an object;
but if the dharma is without an object, how then can there be an object again?
When phenomena have not arisen, cessation is not possible; therefore, an immediate [condition] is not logical. Furthermore, what condition could there be for that which has already ceased?
Since there is no existence for things that lack intrinsic nature,
the principle "when this exists, that comes to be" is simply not tenable.
Furthermore, that fruit does not exist in the conditions either individually or collectively;
how could that which does not exist in the conditions arise from the conditions?
Now, if that effect, though non-existent, proceeds from those conditions,
why does it not also proceed from non-conditions?
The fruit consists of conditions, yet the conditions themselves do not consist of themselves.
How can that fruit which arises from things that do not consist of themselves consist of conditions?
Therefore, an effect consisting of conditions does not exist, nor one consisting of non-conditions.
Since the effect is absent, how can there be conditions or non-conditions?
That which has already gone is not being traversed; that which has not yet been gone over is certainly not being traversed.
That which is presently being traversed, being free from both what has been traversed and what has not yet been traversed, is not being traversed.
Where there is movement, there is going;

and since that movement occurs in the process of being traversed, and not in what has already been traversed nor in what has not yet been traversed, therefore going is located in the process of being traversed.
How indeed can going belong to that which is being gone over,
when it is not at all possible for there to be a "being-gone-over" that is devoid of going?
For one who holds that there is going within the presently being gone over,
it follows that there is a presently being gone over even without going, for the presently being gone over is indeed being gone over.
If there were motion in that which is currently being traversed, two motions would follow:
that by which it is being traversed, and furthermore, the motion itself therein.
If two acts of going were to be postulated, it would follow that there are two goers;
for indeed, an act of going is not possible apart from a goer.
If going is not possible apart from a goer,
then how indeed can there be a goer when going does not exist?
First, the goer does not go; likewise, the non-goer does not go at all.
Apart from the goer and the non-goer, what third party could possibly go?
How indeed can it be tenable that "the goer goes," when a goer is not at all possible without the act of going?
For one who maintains that "the goer goes," it follows that there is a goer even without going,
since you desire a going that belongs to a goer.
If a goer goes, it would follow that there are two acts of going:
that by which he is designated as a "goer," and that which he who is already a goer performs.
Going does not begin in what has already gone; going does not begin in what has not yet been gone;
it does not begin in the process of going. Where, then, does going begin?

Prior to the commencement of going, there is neither a path being traversed nor a path already traversed; where, then, could going begin? For how can there be going in that which has not yet been traversed?
When the commencement of going itself is not perceived in any way whatsoever, what is the gone, what is the being-gone-over, and what is the not-yet-gone that can be conceptualized?
The goer does not stand still, nor indeed does the non-goer stand still;
what third party, other than the goer and the non-goer, could then stand still?
How indeed can it be tenable that "the goer stands"?
For when a goer is not possible at all without the act of going.
Motion does not exist in that which is being traversed, nor in what has been traversed, nor even in what has not yet been traversed;
the commencement and cessation of motion are the same as those of the traversed.
That the goer is identical to the act of going is not tenable;
furthermore, that the goer is something other than the act of going is also not tenable.
For if the act of going were indeed identical to the goer,
it would follow that the agent and the action are one and the same.
If, on the other hand, the goer is conceptualized as being entirely distinct from the act of going,
then there would be going without a goer, and there would be a goer without going.
For those two for whom establishment is found neither through identity nor through difference,
how indeed can their establishment exist?
By means of whatever going a goer is designated, he does not go by that very going;
for there is no one whatsoever who exists prior to going, since it is only someone [already existing] who goes.
By means of that going by which a goer is designated, he does not go by another;
for two goings are not possible in a single goer.
One who exists as a real entity does not undergo the threefold going;
nor does one who does not exist as a real entity undergo that threefold going.
One who exists, one who does not exist, and one who both exists and does not exist do not go in any of the three ways.
Therefore, going, the goer, and the destination do not exist.
Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind—
There are these six sense faculties; their objective domain consists of the visible objects and so forth.
For that vision does not see its own self;
how can that which does not see itself see other things?
The analogy of fire is not sufficient to establish vision;
for that [fire] which possesses vision has already been refuted by the analysis of the traversed, the untraversed, and the being-traversed.
When there is no seeing whatsoever of that which is not being seen,
how can it be tenable to say, "seeing sees"?
Vision does not see at all, nor does non-vision see;
by means of vision itself, the seer has also been explained and should be understood.
There is no seer apart from seeing, nor is there one who includes seeing;
since the seer does not exist, how can there be that which is seen and seeing itself?
Just as the arising of a son is said to occur in dependence upon a mother and a father,
so too is the arising of consciousness said to occur in dependence upon the eye and visible form.
Since there is no seeing of that which is to be seen, the tetrad beginning with consciousness does not exist; how then will grasping and the subsequent factors come to be?
Hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the mind have been explained;
one should understand the hearer, the object of hearing, and so forth, by means of the very same analysis applied to seeing.
Form is not perceived as something separate from the cause of form.
The cause of form is not seen to be devoid of form itself.
If form were devoid of the cause of form, it would follow that form is causeless;
yet no object whatsoever exists anywhere that is without a cause.
If the cause of form were to exist apart from form itself, it would be a cause without an effect;
yet there is no cause that lacks an effect.
When form exists, a cause of form is not tenable;
when form does not exist, a cause of form is not tenable.
Furthermore, form that is without a cause is simply not possible at all.
Therefore, one should not conceptualize any conceptual constructions regarding form.
It is not tenable that the effect is similar to the cause;
nor is it tenable that the effect is dissimilar to the cause.
The sequence for sensation, mind, perception, and mental formations, as well as for all entities whatsoever, is in every respect identical to that of form.
In a debate, whatever rebuttal one might offer when emptiness has been established, all of that remains unanswered and turns out to be equivalent to the very point to be proven.

In an exposition, whatever objection one might raise against that which has been established through emptiness, all of that remains unrefuted, as it becomes equal to the very point to be proven. Space does not exist at all prior to the characteristic of space.
If it were to exist prior to its characteristic, it would follow that it is without a characteristic.
Nowhere does there exist any entity whatsoever that is without characteristics;
since an entity without characteristics does not exist, where could a characteristic possibly apply?
The activity of a characteristic does not occur in that which lacks a characteristic, nor in that which possesses a characteristic;
it does not proceed from anything other than that which possesses a characteristic or that which lacks a characteristic.
And when the characteristic does not occur, the characterized object is not tenable;
and when the characterized object is not tenable, the characteristic itself is impossible.
Therefore, the characterized does not exist, nor indeed does the characteristic exist;
apart from the characterized and the characteristic, even an entity (bhāva) does not exist at all.
And if an entity does not exist, of what will there be non-existence?
Furthermore, who is there that possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence and can perceive existence and non-existence?
Therefore, space is neither an entity nor a non-entity, neither the characterized nor the characteristic;
the other five elements are likewise equal to space.

But those of small intelligence who perceive existence and non-existence do not see the auspicious tranquility of all things, which is the true object of vision. If the one who is impassioned were to exist prior to passion, he would exist as something independent of passion.
Dependent upon that, passion would come to be; passion exists when there is one who is impassioned.
Furthermore, if the one who is attached does not exist, how indeed will attachment come to be?
Whether attachment exists or does not exist, this same sequence applies to the one who is attached as well.
Furthermore, the simultaneous arising of passion and the impassioned one is not tenable;
for passion and the impassioned one would then exist independently of each other.
In identity, there is no coexistence, for a thing cannot exist together with itself;
in difference, how indeed could coexistence come to be?
If coexistence were to exist in identity, it would exist even without a companion;
if coexistence were to exist in difference, it would exist even without a companion.
If there were coexistence in separateness, what would be established as the separate existence of passion and the impassioned one, such that there could be their coexistence?
If the separate existence of passion and the impassioned one is established,
for what purpose do you nevertheless imagine their coexistence?
Thinking that it is not established as separate, you thus desire simultaneous existence;
yet for the sake of establishing simultaneous existence, you further desire separateness.
And since separate existence is not established, coexistence is not established either;
in what kind of separate existence do you desire coexistence to exist?
Thus, the establishment of passion through one who is impassioned is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous;
as with passion, the establishment of all phenomena is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous.
If arising were conditioned, then the three characteristics would be applicable to it.
Now, if arising were unconditioned, how could it be a characteristic of the conditioned?
The three [characteristics] beginning with arising, when taken separately, are not capable of performing the function of defining the conditioned;
how could they exist together in a single place at one time?
If there exists another characteristic of the conditioned for arising, duration, and destruction, there would be an infinite regress; if it does not exist, then they are not conditioned.
The arising of arising is merely the arising of the primary arising;
furthermore, the primary arising brings about the arising of arising.
If, according to you, the "arising of arising" is the arising of the fundamental arising,
then how will that [secondary arising], which has not been produced by the fundamental [arising], produce it?
If that [subsequent] fundamental [arising] produces the fundamental [arising] which was produced by the fundamental one,
how can that fundamental [arising], not having been produced by it, produce it?
If this [fire], while being produced, could produce that [fuel]—
provided that this [fire], being unborn, were capable of producing it— then indeed it might produce it.
Just as a lamp illuminates both itself and other things,
so too arising should produce both itself and other things.
There is no darkness in a lamp, nor where it is situated.
What does the lamp illuminate? For illumination is simply the destruction of darkness.
How is darkness destroyed by a lamp as it is arising?
For when the lamp is arising, it does not reach the darkness.
Or if darkness were destroyed by a lamp without even reaching it,
then a lamp situated here would destroy the darkness existing throughout the entire world.
If a lamp illuminates both itself and others,
then darkness, too, will undoubtedly conceal both itself and others.
How could this arising, being unarisen, produce itself?
Or, if it produces while already arisen, what is produced once it has already been born?
That which is not being produced, not already produced, and not yet unproduced is in no way produced;
this has been explained by means of the concepts of the present process of going, the gone, and the not-yet-gone.
When this "presently arising" does not apply to the process of arising,
how can it be said that the presently arising arises in dependence upon arising?
Whatever arises dependently is by its very nature quiescent;
therefore, that which is arising and arising itself are likewise quiescent.
If some unarisen entity were found anywhere, it might arise; but since that entity does not exist, what is it that arises?
If this arising, while itself arising, causes that [other] arising to arise,
then what further arising would cause that arising to arise?
If another produces this production, there would be an infinite regress;
but if that which is unproduced is produced, then everything should likewise be produced in that same way.
The arising of that which exists, of that which does not exist, or of that which both exists and does not exist is not tenable; this has already been established previously.
The arising of an entity that is in the process of ceasing is not tenable;
nor is an entity that is not in the process of ceasing tenable.
An entity that has not yet stayed does not stay; an entity that has already stayed does not stay.
That which is currently staying does not stay; and what unarisen thing stays?
The persistence of an entity that is currently ceasing is not tenable;
nor is an entity that is not ceasing at all tenable.
Since all entities always possess the nature of aging and death,
what entities are there that exist without aging and death?
The abiding of abiding by means of another abiding, or by that very same [abiding], is not tenable;
just as the arising of arising is neither through itself nor through another.
That which has not ceased does not cease, nor does that which has already ceased cease;
likewise, that which is currently ceasing [does not cease]. Furthermore, how could that which is unborn cease?
The cessation of an entity that is currently abiding is not tenable;
nor is the cessation of an entity that is not abiding tenable.
Indeed, a state is not ceased by that very same state;
nor is a state ceased by a different state. MMK 7.28.
When the arising of all phenomena is not tenable,
then likewise the cessation of all phenomena is not tenable.
Furthermore, the cessation of an existent entity is not tenable;
for if there were identity, neither existence nor non-existence would be possible.
The cessation of even a non-existent entity is not tenable,
just as the cutting off of a second head does not occur.
Cessation does not exist by way of its own nature, nor does cessation exist by way of another nature;
just as the arising of arising is neither by way of itself nor by way of another.
Since arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established, the conditioned does not exist;
and since the conditioned is not established, how will the unconditioned be established?
Just as an illusion, just as a dream, and just as a city of the Gandharvas,
so have arising, abiding, and ceasing been described.
An agent that is truly existent does not perform an action that is truly existent.
Nor does an agent who is non-existent strive after an action that is non-existent.
For that which is truly existent, there is no action, and there would be karma without an agent;
for that which is truly existent, there is no action, and there would be an agent without karma.
If an unreal agent were to perform an unreal action,
then the action would be without a cause, and the agent would also be without a cause.
When a cause does not exist, neither effect nor cause is found;
in their absence, action, agent, and instrument are not found.
When action and so forth are impossible, neither merit nor demerit exist;
and when merit and demerit do not exist, the fruit born from them does not exist.
If the fruit does not exist, the path leading to liberation or to heaven is untenable;
furthermore, it follows that all purposeful actions would be rendered meaningless.
An agent who is both existent and non-existent does not produce that which is both existent and non-existent;
for how can the existent and the non-existent, being mutually contradictory, exist as one?
That which exists is not produced by that which does not exist, nor is that which exists produced by that which does not exist;
for in that case, all those very same faults would necessarily follow for the agent.
By the very reasons previously stated, an agent does not perform an action that is non-existent, nor one that is existent, nor one that is both existent and non-existent.
An agent that is non-existent does not perform an action that is existent, nor one that is both existent and non-existent; this is due to the very reasons previously stated.
An agent who is both existent and non-existent does not perform an action that is existent or non-existent;
one should understand this by means of the very reasons previously stated.
The agent exists in dependence upon the action, and the action proceeds in dependence upon that agent;
we see no other means for their establishment.
Thus one should understand appropriation through the relinquishing of action and agent;
by means of action and agent, one should analyze the remaining entities.
Furthermore, [one should analyze] seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth.
Some indeed say that he to whom these [aggregates] previously belong exists.
For how could seeing and the other [sensory functions] belong to a thing that does not exist?
Therefore, prior to these, that thing exists as an established entity.
Furthermore, by what means is that entity which existed prior to seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, designated?
If he were established even without seeing and the other [faculties],
then these too would undoubtedly exist without him.
Someone is anointed by something; something is anointed by someone.
Without something, how can there be someone? Without someone, how can there be something?
No one exists prior to all [the functions] such as seeing and so forth;
rather, at different times, one [function] among seeing and the rest is manifested by means of another.
If he does not exist prior to all [faculties] such as vision,
how can he exist prior to each individual one, such as vision?
If that very same one is the seer, that very same one is the hearer, and that very same one is the feeler, then [the self] would exist prior to each [activity]; however, this is not tenable.
If, moreover, the seer were one, the hearer another, and the knower yet another,
then while there is a seer, there would also be a hearer, and there would be a plurality of selves.
Furthermore, this [self] is not found even in those elements from which seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth, arise.
If that to which seeing, hearing, and so forth, as well as feeling and so forth belong,
does not exist, then these [functions] do not exist either.

That which does not exist prior to seeing and the other [sensory functions], nor at present, nor even in the future— regarding that, the conceptual constructions of "it exists" and "it does not exist" have ceased.
If that which is the fuel were the fire, there would be identity between the agent and the object.
If fire were other than fuel, it would exist even without fuel.
It would be eternally aflame, lacking any cause for its ignition;
furthermore, in such a case, the act of starting it would be useless, and it would be devoid of action.
Because it would not depend on anything else, it would follow that fire is without a cause for its ignition;
furthermore, if it were eternally burning, the act of kindling it again would be rendered useless.
In this regard, it might be argued that "the fuel is that which is being burned.
But by what could that fuel be burned when it is merely that [fuel] itself? (MMK 10.4)
One who has not attained will not attain; one who does not burn will not be extinguished;
and one who is not unextinguished will either remain or persist with its own characteristic.
If fire were something entirely other than its fuel, it would reach the fuel, just as a woman reaches a man and a man reaches a woman. (MMK 10.6)
Fire would indeed be something other than fuel, and it might reach the fuel,
if fire and fuel were mutually independent of one another.
If fire depends on fuel, and if fuel depends on fire,
which of the two is established first, such that fire depends on it as fuel?
If fire were established in dependence upon fuel, then that which is already established would be the proof of fire;
and if this were so, fuel too would exist without fire.
If an entity is established in dependence upon something else, and that very thing in turn is established in dependence upon it, then let that which is to be depended upon be established;
but depending upon what could what be established?
If an entity is established in dependence [on another], how can that which is unestablished depend?
On the other hand, if it is already established, its dependence is not tenable.
Fire does not exist in dependence on fuel, nor does fire exist independent of fuel;
fuel does not exist in dependence on fire, nor does fuel exist independent of fire.
Fire does not come from elsewhere, nor is fire found within the fuel;
regarding this fuel, the rest has been explained by means of [the analysis of] the being-traversed, the traversed, and the untraversed.
Furthermore, fuel is not fire, nor is fire elsewhere than from fuel;
fire does not possess fuel, fuel is not in fire, nor is fire in them.
The sequence regarding the self and its appropriation has been explained by means of fire and fuel;
it applies entirely and without exception to all things, including pots, cloths, and so forth.
Those who point to a self-essence of the self and of phenomena as being distinct from one another— I do not consider them to be experts in the meaning of the teaching.
The Great Sage said that a prior limit is not known.
For cyclic existence is indeed without beginning or end; it has neither a first nor a last.
For that which has neither beginning nor end, how could there be a middle?
Therefore, in this case, the sequences of prior, posterior, and simultaneous do not occur.
If birth were to exist first and old age and death were to follow later,
then birth would occur without old age and death, and one who is immortal would be born.
If birth were to occur later and old age and death at the beginning,
how could there be old age and death for that which is unborn, being thus without a cause?
Neither is aging-and-death joined with birth;
for if it were so, one would be dying while being born, and both would be without cause.
Where these sequences of prior, posterior, and simultaneous do not prevail,
how could they proliferate that birth, or that old age and death?
Effect and cause, as well as the characterized and the characteristic,
sensation and the feeler— whatever objects there may be [are likewise non-existent].
Not only is a prior limit of cyclic existence not found,
but for all phenomena as well, a prior limit does not exist.
[It is] self-made, made by another, made by both, or without cause.
Some maintain that suffering exists; however, it is not logical for that [suffering] to be an effect.
If it were self-made, it would not arise dependently;
for indeed, these aggregates arise in dependence upon those aggregates.
If these were different from those, or if those were other than these, then suffering would be produced by another; for these [beings] would have been created by those others.
If suffering were created by one's own person, then what is that person who exists independently of suffering,
by whom that suffering was self-created?
If suffering produced by another person is given to someone else after having been created by that other, how could that [other] exist without suffering? (MMK 12.5)
If suffering is produced by another person, who is that other person who,
being himself devoid of suffering, creates it and sends it to another?
Since that which is self-made is not established, how can suffering be made by another?
For if another were to produce the suffering, that would be [for him] self-made.
Suffering is not first of all self-made, for it is not made by that very same thing;
if the other were not self-made, how could suffering be made by another?
If suffering were produced by both, or if it were produced by each one individually,
how could there be suffering that is neither caused by another nor self-caused, and which is thus without a cause?

For not only does the fourfold nature of suffering not exist, but even the fourfold nature of external entities does not exist. That which has a deceptive nature is false; thus the Blessed One has said.
And all conditioned phenomena have the nature of deception; therefore, they are false.
If that which has the nature of deception is false, what is it therein that is deceived?
This, however, was stated by the Blessed One as an illumination of emptiness.
The lack of intrinsic nature in entities is due to the observation of their alteration;
for there is no entity that lacks intrinsic nature, since emptiness is the very nature of entities.
If intrinsic nature does not exist, of what could there be alteration?
If intrinsic nature does exist, of what could there be alteration?
Neither the change of that very thing nor the change of something else is tenable;
for a youth does not age, and likewise, one who is already aged does not age.
If there were a transformation of that [milk], then milk itself would be curd;
otherwise, some thing other than milk would become curd.
If there were something non-empty, then there might be something called empty;
but since there is nothing whatsoever that is non-empty, how will there be an empty?
Emptiness was taught by the Victors as the relinquishing of all views;
but those for whom emptiness itself is a view were declared to be incurable.
The object of vision, the act of seeing, and the seer— these three do not enter into a relationship with one another either two by two or all together.
In this way, let passion, the impassioned one, and the object of passion be seen;
by means of these three, the remaining afflictions and the remaining sense-bases are also to be understood.
The conjunction of one thing with another presupposes that otherness;
however, such otherness does not exist among the objects of sight and so forth, and therefore they do not enter into conjunction.
Not only does otherness not exist for the seen object and so forth;
otherness is not tenable for anything whatsoever in relation to anything else.
One thing is dependent on another; one thing is not other than another without [that] other.
And that which is dependent upon something else—therefore, it is not logically tenable for it to be other [than that].
If one thing were other than another, it would exist even without that other; yet no such "other" exists without the other, and therefore it does not exist.
Difference does not exist in that which is other, nor does it exist in that which is not other.
Since difference does not exist, neither "other" nor "that very thing" exists.
The conjunction of that with itself is not possible, nor is the conjunction of one thing with another;
neither the process of conjoining, the conjoined, nor the conjoiner exists.
It is not logical for intrinsic nature (svabhāva) to arise from causes and conditions.
An intrinsic nature produced from causes and conditions would be something created.
Furthermore, how could intrinsic nature be something produced?
For intrinsic nature is non-artificial and independent of anything else.
How, in the absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), could there be extrinsic nature (parabhāva)?
For intrinsic nature is indeed said to be the extrinsic nature of another.
Apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, how could an entity possibly exist?
For an entity is established only when intrinsic nature or extrinsic nature exists.
If existence is not established, non-existence is certainly not established;
for people describe the alteration of existence as non-existence.
Those who perceive intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, as well as existence and non-existence, do not perceive the reality in the Buddha's teaching.
And in the *Kātyāyanāvavāda*, both "it exists" and "it does not exist" were refuted by the Blessed One, who perceives both existence and non-existence.
If existence were by way of intrinsic nature, its non-existence would not occur;
for it is never possible for there to be a change in intrinsic nature.
If intrinsic nature does not exist, for what will there be alteration?
Or, if intrinsic nature exists, for what will there be alteration? (MMK 15.9)
"It exists" is the grasping at eternalism; "it does not exist" is the view of nihilism.
Therefore, the wise person should not rely upon existence or non-existence.
For that which exists by way of its own-nature (svabhāva) cannot be non-existent; thus, eternalism (śāśvata) follows.
To say "it does not exist now, though it existed previously" entails the consequence of annihilationism (uccheda).
If it is argued that the conditioned factors (saṃskāra) transmigrate, they do not transmigrate as permanent entities.
And they transmigrate as non-eternal; this same sequence applies to sentient beings as well.
If it is the person who transmigrates within the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, that person cannot be found when sought in five ways; who then will transmigrate?
Transmigrating from one grasping to another, one would become non-existent;
and being non-existent and without grasping, who is that person and what will transmigrate?
The nirvāṇa of conditioned phenomena is not possible in any way;
the nirvāṇa of a sentient being is also not possible in any way.
Formations, being subject to the nature of arising and passing away, are neither bound nor liberated; as before, a sentient being is neither bound nor liberated.
If grasping is the bondage, then one who possesses grasping is not bound;
nor is one who lacks grasping bound. In what state, then, is one bound?
One might indeed bind that which is being bound, if it were to exist prior to being bound;
however, such a thing does not exist, as has been explained by the analysis of the traversed, the untraversed, and that which is currently being traversed.
One who is bound is not liberated, nor indeed is one who is unbound liberated.
If the bound were being liberated, there would be simultaneous bondage and liberation.
"For those who hold the grasping thought, 'I shall attain nirvāṇa without clinging; nirvāṇa will be mine,' their grasping is a great obsession."
There is no superimposition of nirvana, nor any removal of samsara.
Where [these do not exist], what samsara is there, and what nirvana is conceptualized?
That mind which restrains itself and favors others— that loving-kindness is the dharma, the seed of fruit both hereafter and in this world.
The Supreme Sage has stated that action consists of volition and what is performed after having willed;
he has fully proclaimed many varieties of that action.
In that regard, what is called "volition" (cetanā) is known as mental action;
whereas what is called "having willed" (cetayitvā) is both bodily and vocal action.
The vibrations of speech and those non-abstinences designated as "non-informative" (avijñapti),
as well as other non-informative [factors] known as abstinences, are likewise [unreal].
Merit resulting from enjoyment, demerit of the same kind,
and volition— these seven factors are traditionally taught as the manifestations of karma.
If the action remains until the time of ripening, it would follow that it is eternal;
if it has ceased, being already ceased, how will it produce a fruit?
The continuum beginning with the sprout that proceeds from the seed does not proceed from that [continuum] once the seed is absent;
yet, without the seed, it does not proceed at all.
Since the continuum arises from the seed, and the production of the fruit arises from the continuum, the fruit has the seed as its precursor; therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
That continuum of mind which proceeds from that [mind],
and from which the fruit arises— without the mind, it does not proceed.
Since the continuum arises from the mind, and the arising of the fruit arises from the continuum,
the fruit preceded by karma is therefore neither annihilated nor eternal.
The ten white paths of action are the means for accomplishing dharma;
the fruit of dharma consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure both in this world and after death.
If this conceptual construction were to exist, there would be many and great faults;
therefore, this conceptual construction is simply not tenable here.
Furthermore, I shall now set forth this conceptual formulation which is applicable here,
and which has been praised by the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas.
Just as a promissory note is not lost, so too is karma like a debt;
it is fourfold according to the realms, and by its very nature, it is indeterminate.
It is not to be abandoned through abandonment, nor is it to be abandoned through cultivation;
therefore, the fruit of actions arises by means of non-perishing.
If [an action] were to be abandoned through its abandonment or by the transference of the action,
then faults such as the destruction of action would follow.
At the moment of rebirth-linking, among all the dissimilar and similar karmas belonging to the same realm, only one of them arises.
That [result] arises in the present life from every kind of action; furthermore, it persists even when the two types of action have ripened.
It ceases either through the transcendence of its fruit or through death;
therein one should discern the distinction between that which is with outflows and that which is without outflows.
Emptiness is not annihilation, and cyclic existence is not eternal;
the non-perishing of karma—this is the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Why does karma not arise? Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature. And because it is unarisen, for that reason it does not perish.
If karma were to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature, it would undoubtedly be eternal.
Furthermore, karma would be uncreated, for that which is eternal is not produced through action.
If action were uncreated, there would be the fear of encountering the results of what one has not done;
furthermore, the fault of not living the holy life (abrahmacarya) would follow in that case.
All worldly conventions would undoubtedly be contradicted;
furthermore, the distinction between the doer of merit and the doer of evil would not be tenable.
Furthermore, that which has already ripened as its maturation would ripen yet again;
since karma is established [as such], it would therefore possess an intrinsic nature.
This [world] consists of karma and afflictions, yet those afflictions do not exist in reality.
If those afflictions do not exist in reality, how could karma exist in reality?
Karma and the afflictions are declared to be the conditions for bodies;
if karma and the afflictions are empty, what can be said of bodies?
The living being is obscured by ignorance and bound by craving;
he is the enjoyer, yet he is neither different from the agent nor is he that very same person.
Since this action does not arise from conditions nor is it unarisen from conditions,
therefore the agent also does not exist.
If there is neither action nor an agent, from where could there be a fruit born of action?
And if the fruit does not exist, how indeed will there be an experiencer?
Just as the Teacher, by means of his perfected supernatural power, might create a magical emanation,
and that emanation might in turn create another emanation— so too is this [case].
Likewise, the agent who has the form of a magical creation performs an action that is itself like a creation;
just as one magical creation is created by another magical creation.

Afflictions, actions, bodies, agents, and fruits are like the form of a city of Gandharvas; they resemble a mirage or a dream. If the self were the aggregates, it would be subject to arising and passing away.
If it were other than the aggregates, it would lack the characteristics of the aggregates.
When the self does not exist, how indeed can that which belongs to the self exist?
Through the pacification of both the self and what pertains to the self, one is free from "mine-ness" and free from "I-ness."
That which is without "mine-ness" and without "I-ness" does not exist either;
he who perceives that which is without "mine-ness" and without "I-ness" does not perceive.
When "mine" and "I" have ceased, both externally and internally, grasping is extinguished;
through the destruction of that, there is the destruction of birth.
Liberation comes from the exhaustion of karma and afflictions; karma and afflictions arise from conceptual construction;
these arise from conceptual proliferation; but conceptual proliferation ceases in emptiness.
The Buddhas have designated "self," they have taught "non-self," and they have also taught that there is neither self nor non-self whatsoever.
That which is to be designated has ceased; the range of the mind has ceased.
For the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed unarisen and unceasing, like nirvāṇa.
"All is real, or not real, both real and unreal,
and neither unreal nor real— this is the instruction of the Buddhas."
Not dependent on another, peaceful, not proliferated by conceptual proliferations, free from discursive thought, and without manifold meanings— this is the characteristic of reality.
Whatever arises dependently is indeed not that very thing, nor is it something other than it;
therefore, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Neither manifold nor diverse, neither annihilated nor eternal—
this is the nectar of the teaching of the Buddhas, the Lords of the World.
In the absence of the appearance of fully awakened Buddhas and upon the passing away of the disciples,
the knowledge of the Pratyekabuddhas arises from solitude.
If the present and the future exist in dependence upon the past, [then they must exist within it].
The present and the future will exist within the time of the past.
If, moreover, the present and the future do not exist there [in the past],
how could the present and the future exist in dependence upon it?
Furthermore, the establishment of those two does not exist without depending on the past;
therefore, neither the present nor the future time exists.
By this very same [method], one should characterize the two remaining [alternatives] in their respective order—
the superior, the inferior, and the intermediate, as well as oneness and so forth— as being subject to exchange.
Time that is not abiding cannot be grasped; time that is abiding does not exist.
How can time be designated if it is neither being grasped nor has been grasped?
If time exists dependent upon an entity, how can there be time apart from an entity?
Since no entity whatsoever exists, how will time come to be?
And if [an effect] were born from the assemblage of causes and conditions...
And yet the fruit exists within the causal complex; how then can it be produced by that complex?
If the fruit arises from the assemblage of causes and conditions,
and yet that fruit does not exist within the assemblage, how can it arise from the assemblage?
If the effect existed within the assemblage of causes and conditions, it would surely be perceived within that assemblage;
yet it is not perceived within the assemblage.
If the effect does not exist within the assemblage of causes and conditions,
then those causes and conditions would be the same as non-causes and non-conditions.
If the cause were to cease after having given the cause for the fruit, then there would be a twofold nature of the cause: that which was given and that which ceased.
And if the cause were to cease without having imparted its causal efficiency to the effect,
then that effect, being born when the cause has ceased, would be without a cause.
If the fruit were to manifest simultaneously with the causal complex,
it would follow that the producer and that which is produced exist at the same time.
Furthermore, if the fruit were to manifest prior to the causal complex itself,
then the fruit would be devoid of causes and conditions, and thus would be causeless.
If the effect were to exist when the cause has already ceased, there would be a transference of the cause;
furthermore, it would follow that a cause already previously born would undergo birth again.
How could a cause that has ceased and passed away produce an arisen fruit?
And even if it were to persist, how could a cause produce a fruit when it is obstructed by it?
Furthermore, being unaccompanied by a fruit, what kind of fruit could it produce?
For a cause does not produce a fruit either by not having seen [the fruit] or by having seen it.
For a past effect, there is never found any conjunction with a past cause,
nor with one that is unborn, nor with one that has already arisen.
For there is never found a conjunction of an arisen effect with an unarisen cause,
nor with one that is past, nor with one that has already arisen.
For there is never any conjunction of a non-arisen effect with a cause that is either arisen, non-arisen, or destroyed.
If there is no conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect?
Or, if there is a conjunction, how can a cause produce an effect?
If the cause is empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect?
If the cause is not empty of the effect, how can it produce the effect?
A non-empty fruit will not arise, and a non-empty fruit will not cease.
That which is non-empty would be neither ceased nor arisen.
How can that which is empty arise? How can that which is empty cease?
It follows that even the empty would be unceased and unarisen.
The identity of cause and effect is never tenable;
likewise, the difference between cause and effect is never tenable.
If cause and effect were identical, there would be oneness between the producer and the produced;
if cause and effect were distinct, a cause would be equivalent to a non-cause.
How will a cause produce an effect that exists by way of its own nature? How will a cause produce an effect that does not exist by way of its own nature?
And for that which does not produce [an effect], the status of being a cause is not tenable;
and if the status of being a cause is untenable, whose fruit will there be?
Furthermore, how could that collection of conditions and causes— which does not produce itself by means of itself— produce an effect?
The fruit is not produced by the causal complex, nor is the fruit produced by what is not a causal complex.
Since the causal complex itself does not exist without a fruit, how could it exist?
Indeed, disintegration does not exist either with or without origination.
There is indeed no possibility of arising either without or together with destruction.
How indeed could there be dissolution without origination?
There can be no death without birth; dissolution does not exist without emergence.
How could passing away exist simultaneously with arising?
For birth and death are not found to occur at the same time.
How indeed could there be arising without passing away?
For impermanence is never not found among existing things.
How can arising exist together with destruction?
For birth and death are not found to occur at the same time.
If for two things there is no establishment either together with one another or without one another, how indeed can their establishment exist?
There is no arising of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there an arising of that which is not subject to destruction.
There is no passing away of that which is subject to destruction, nor is there a passing away of that which is not subject to destruction.
Neither origination nor destruction exists without an entity;
likewise, neither origination nor destruction exists without an entity.
Neither arising nor passing away is possible for that which is empty;
neither arising nor passing away is possible for that which is non-empty.
It is not tenable that origination and dissolution are one and the same;
nor is it tenable that origination and dissolution are different.
Both arising and passing away would be perceived by you;
yet it is only through delusion that both arising and passing away are perceived.
An entity does not arise from an entity, nor does an entity arise from a non-entity;
a non-entity does not arise from a non-entity, nor does a non-entity arise from an entity.
An entity is not born from itself, nor indeed is it born from another;
it is not born from both itself and another—how then could it be born?
For one who has accepted existence, the views of eternalism and nihilism follow as a consequence;
for that existence must be either permanent or impermanent.
For one who has accepted existence, there is neither annihilation nor permanence;
for existence is indeed the continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect.
If existence were a continuum of the arising and passing away of cause and effect,
it would follow that because what has passed away does not arise again, there would be a total cessation of the cause.
Furthermore, it is not logical for non-existence to exist by way of its own intrinsic nature;
moreover, at the time of nirvāṇa, there would be annihilation due to the cessation of the continuum of existence.
The first existence is not tenable when the last has ceased,
nor is the first existence tenable when the last has not ceased.
If the first were to arise while the last is ceasing,
then that which is ceasing would be one thing, and that which is arising would be another.
If it is not logical for that which is ceasing and that which is arising to exist simultaneously within those very aggregates in which one dies, then one is born within them.
Thus, the continuity of existence is not tenable in any of the three times.
How can that which does not exist in the three times be the continuity of existence?
He is not the aggregates, nor is he other than the aggregates; the aggregates are not in him, nor is he in them.
The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates; which, then, in this case, is the Tathāgata?
If the Buddha, depending upon the aggregates, does not exist by way of intrinsic nature,
how can he exist by way of extrinsic nature when he does not exist by way of intrinsic nature?
That which exists in dependence upon another nature is established as being non-self;
and how can that which is non-self be the Tathāgata?
If intrinsic nature does not exist, how could extrinsic nature exist? Apart from intrinsic nature and extrinsic nature, who is that Tathāgata?
If there were some Tathāgata existing without depending upon the aggregates, he would now have to depend [upon them]; therefore, he exists by depending [upon them].
Furthermore, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever who exists without depending upon the aggregates;
and how can that which does not exist without depending [upon them] ever come to depend [upon them]?
There is no appropriation whatsoever that is not appropriated,
nor does a Tathāgata exist in any way whatsoever without appropriation.
How can that Tathāgata be designated by means of appropriation, when he does not exist as either identical to or different from [the aggregates], even when sought in five ways?
Even this appropriation does not exist by way of intrinsic nature;
and that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature, how could it exist by way of extrinsic nature?
Thus, appropriation and the appropriator are entirely empty;
yet, by means of what is empty, [the Tathāgata] is designated. How, then, can the Tathāgata be empty?
"One should not say 'it is empty,' nor that 'it is non-empty,' nor both, nor neither; yet it is spoken for the sake of conventional designation."
How can the tetrad of eternal, non-eternal, and so forth exist here in that which is peaceful?
And how can the tetrad of finite, infinite, and so forth exist here in that which is peaceful?
But he who has grasped the Tathāgata with a dense clinging, thinking "he exists," while conceptualizing "he does not exist," would likewise conceptualize [him] even after he has passed into nirvāṇa.
Since this [Buddha] is empty by nature,
the thought that "the Buddha exists after cessation" or "does not exist" is simply not tenable.
Those who conceptualize the Buddha, who is beyond conceptual proliferation and undecaying, are all destroyed by conceptual proliferation and do not see the Tathāgata.
Whatever is the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata, that is the intrinsic nature of this world.
The Tathāgata is without intrinsic nature; this world is without intrinsic nature. Passion, hatred, and delusion are said to originate from conceptual construction.
For it is indeed in dependence upon the beautiful, the ugly, and the perversions that they arise.
Those afflictions which arise dependent upon the beautiful, the ugly, and the perverted do not exist by way of intrinsic nature; therefore, the afflictions do not exist in reality.
The existence and non-existence of the self are not established in any way whatsoever;
without that [self], how could the existence and non-existence of the afflictions be established?
For these afflictions belong to someone, yet that person is not established;
or rather, do the afflictions exist without anyone, belonging to no one at all?
As with the view of a self-body, the afflictions do not exist in the afflicted in five ways;
as with the view of a self-body, the afflicted also does not exist in the afflictions in five ways.
Intrinsic nature does not exist for the errors of purity and impurity;
dependent upon what errors of purity and impurity could the afflictions arise?
Form, sound, taste, touch, smell, and mental objects—
these sixfold entities are conceptualized as the basis for attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Form, sound, taste, touch, smell,
and mental phenomena alone are like the city of the Gandharvas, resembling a mirage or a dream.
How could there be either the unwholesome or the wholesome in those which are like illusory persons and equal to reflections?
Without depending on the beautiful, the ugly does not exist, which we might designate;
since the beautiful exists in dependence [upon it], therefore the beautiful is simply not tenable.
Without depending on the impure, we could not designate the pure;
since it exists in dependence upon the impure, therefore the impure does not exist at all.
And when the pleasant does not exist, from where will passion arise?
And when the unpleasant does not exist, from where will aversion arise?
If the apprehension of the permanent in the impermanent is a perversion,
then since nothing impermanent exists in emptiness, how can there be such an apprehension or perversion?
If the apprehension of the permanent in the impermanent is a misconception,
why is the apprehension of even the "impermanent" not a misconception in regard to the empty?
That by which one grasps, that which is the grasping, the grasper, and that which is grasped—all these are utterly stilled; therefore, no grasping exists.
If grasping does not exist— whether it be false or even correct—
to whom would there be perversion, and to whom would there be non-perversion?
Furthermore, errors do not occur for one who is already mistaken,
nor do errors occur for one who is not mistaken.
Errors do not occur for one who is currently in error;
consider for yourself for whom errors could possibly occur.
How indeed could errors exist if they are unarisen? If errors have not been produced, how can there be one who possesses error?
An entity is not born from itself, nor is it born from another;
it is not born from both self and other—how, then, could one who has fallen into such views be subject to error?
If a self were pure, eternal, and blissful, then that self would not be a misconception;
for purity, eternity, and bliss would be its true nature.
If neither a self, nor purity, nor permanence,
nor happiness exists, then neither non-self, nor impurity, nor impermanence, nor suffering can exist either.
In this way, ignorance ceases through the cessation of its misconceptions;
when ignorance has ceased, the formative forces and the rest cease.
If any afflictions whatsoever were to exist by way of intrinsic nature for anyone, how indeed could they be abandoned? Who can abandon intrinsic nature?

If any afflictions whatsoever were non-existent by way of intrinsic nature for anyone, how indeed could they be abandoned? Who would abandon that which has no existence? If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away.
It follows that for you, the non-existence of the four noble truths would result.
Full comprehension, abandonment, cultivation,
and realization would not be possible due to the non-existence of the four noble truths.
In the absence of that [the path], the four noble fruits do not exist;
and in the absence of the fruits, there are neither those who abide in the fruits nor those who have entered toward them.
If those eight types of persons do not exist, the Saṅgha does not exist;
and due to the non-existence of the Noble Truths, the True Dharma also does not exist.
When the Dharma and the Saṅgha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha?
By speaking thus, you deny all three jewels.
By [asserting] emptiness, you contradict the existence of the fruits [of action], as well as non-dharma and dharma itself,
and all worldly conventional transactions.
To this we reply: You do not understand the purpose of emptiness, nor emptiness itself, nor the meaning of emptiness; therefore you are thus frustrated. (MMK 24.7)
The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate meaning.
Those who do not understand the distinction between these two truths do not understand the profound reality in the Buddha’s teaching. (MMK 24.9)
Without relying on conventional usage, the ultimate truth is not taught;
without attaining the ultimate truth, nirvana is not realized.
Emptiness, when wrongly perceived, destroys the person of dull intellect,
just as a snake poorly grasped or a spell incorrectly cast.
And for this reason, the Sage’s mind turned away from teaching the Dharma, considering that this Dharma is difficult for the dull-witted to penetrate.
Furthermore, the objection that you raise regarding emptiness does not apply to us, for that consequence of faults does not occur in the case of the empty.
Everything is tenable for him for whom emptiness is tenable;
nothing is tenable for him for whom emptiness is not tenable.
Thus, while attributing your own faults to us,
you have forgotten the very horse upon which you are mounted.
If you perceive the existence of things by way of their intrinsic nature,
then you thereby perceive things as being without causes and conditions.
You negate both effect and cause, as well as the agent, the instrument, and the action;
you negate arising and ceasing, and the fruit as well.
That which is dependent origination, we declare to be emptiness;
it is a dependent designation, and it is itself the middle way.
Since no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not dependently originated,
therefore no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not empty.
If all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
it would follow for you that the four noble truths do not exist.
How could suffering exist if it were not dependently originated?
For that which is impermanent is said to be suffering, and that [impermanence] does not exist in the case of intrinsic nature.
What, moreover, could arise that already exists by way of its own-being?
Therefore, for one who contradicts emptiness, there is no origination.
The cessation of suffering that exists by way of its own intrinsic nature is not possible;
because you maintain the persistence of intrinsic nature, you obstruct cessation.
If the path possesses intrinsic nature, its cultivation is not tenable;
yet if that path is cultivated, for you it lacks intrinsic nature.
When suffering, its origin, and its cessation do not exist,
what path— given that it is for the sake of the cessation of suffering— will bring about [that cessation]?
If there is non-comprehension by way of intrinsic nature, how could there be comprehension of it again?
For surely intrinsic nature is established as permanent.
In this very way, for you, abandonment, realization, and cultivation—
as well as thorough knowledge— are not tenable, nor are the four fruits.
Furthermore, how could a fruit that has not been attained by way of its own-being ever be attainable for one who grasps at an intrinsic nature?
If there is an absence of fruits, there are no those who abide in the fruits, nor are there those who have entered toward them;
if these eight types of persons do not exist, the Saṅgha does not exist.
And because of the non-existence of the Noble Truths, the True Dharma also does not exist;
when the Dharma and the Saṅgha do not exist, how will there be a Buddha?
Furthermore, it would follow for you that enlightenment exists independently of a Buddha, and it would also follow for you that a Buddha exists independently of enlightenment. (MMK 24.31)
And he who is by nature unawakened, even though striving for awakening,
will not attain awakening through the conduct of a bodhisattva.
And no one will ever perform either dharma or adharma;
for what is there to be done with that which is non-empty? Indeed, intrinsic nature is not something that can be produced.
Indeed, for you, there exists a fruit even without dharma and adharma;
yet for you, there exists no fruit that has dharma and adharma as its cause.
Or if you hold that there is a fruit caused by merit and demerit,
how can that fruit produced from merit and demerit be non-empty for you?
And you contradict all worldly conventions because you contradict emptiness, which is dependent origination.
For one who contradicts emptiness, there would be nothing to be done, action would be uninitiated, and an agent would exist without acting.
The world will be unarisen, unceased, and immutable, yet it will exist through various states while being devoid of intrinsic nature.
If it were not empty, there would be no attainment of what has not yet been attained, no action that brings an end to suffering, and no abandonment of all afflictions.
Whoever sees dependent origination sees this:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path itself.
If all this is empty, there is neither arising nor passing away.
Through the abandoning or the cessation of what is nirvāṇa intended?
If all this were non-empty, there would be neither arising nor passing away;
through the abandoning or the cessation of what, then, is nirvāṇa asserted?
Neither abandoned nor attained, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither ceased nor arisen— this is called nirvāṇa.
First of all, nirvāṇa is not an existent entity; for it would follow that it possesses the characteristics of old age and death, since no existent entity exists without old age and death.
And if nirvāṇa were an existent thing, nirvāṇa would be conditioned;
for no existent thing whatsoever is found anywhere that is unconditioned.
And if nirvāṇa were an entity, how could it be non-dependent?
For indeed, no entity whatsoever exists that is not dependent.
If nirvāṇa is not an entity, how will it be a non-entity? Where there is no entity, there no non-entity exists.
If nirvāṇa were a non-entity, how could it be non-dependent?
For there exists no such thing as a non-entity that occurs without dependence.
That which is the state of coming and going, whether by way of grasping or dependent origination—
that, when without grasping and not dependently originated, is taught as nirvāṇa.
The Teacher has declared the abandonment of both existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is logical that nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence.
If nirvāṇa were both existence and non-existence, then liberation would be both existence and non-existence; and that is not tenable.
If nirvāṇa were both an entity and a non-entity,
then nirvāṇa would not be unconditioned, for it would be conditioned by those two.
How could nirvāṇa be both existence and non-existence?
For nirvāṇa is unconditioned, whereas existence and non-existence are conditioned.
How could both existence and non-existence be nirvāṇa?
For the absence of both cannot coexist in one place, like light and darkness.
The teaching that "nirvāṇa is neither non-existence nor existence" is established only when both existence and non-existence are themselves established.
If nirvāṇa exists as neither non-existence nor existence,
by what means is it designated as "neither non-existence nor existence"?
It cannot be asserted that the Blessed One exists after cessation;
nor can it be asserted that he does not exist, or both, or neither.
Even while remaining, the Blessed One is not designated as "existing";
nor is he designated as "not existing," "both," or "neither."
There is no distinction whatsoever of saṃsāra from nirvāṇa;
there is no distinction whatsoever of nirvāṇa from saṃsāra.
The limit of nirvāṇa and the limit of saṃsāra—
between these two, not even the slightest difference is found.
Views concerning the end and so forth, as well as views concerning permanence and so forth, depend upon the state beyond cessation,
the future limit, and the past limit, respectively.
Since all phenomena are empty, what is infinite? What is finite?
What is both infinite and finite? And what is neither infinite nor finite?
Is it that very same thing? Is it something else? Is it eternal? Is it non-eternal?
Is it both non-eternal and eternal? Or is it neither of the two?
The cessation of all apprehension, the cessation of conceptual proliferation, is auspicious.
No dharma whatsoever was taught by the Buddha anywhere to anyone.
[Those] obscured by ignorance perform the threefold formative forces for the sake of renewed existence.
Whatever actions one performs, by those karmas one goes to a particular state of existence.
Consciousness, conditioned by formative forces, descends into a state of existence;
once consciousness has descended, name-and-form is infused.
When name-and-form has been infused, the six sense bases arise;
having reached the six sense bases, contact comes into being.
Depending upon the eye, visible forms, and attention,
and depending likewise upon name-and-form, consciousness thus comes into being.
The conjunction of these three—the eye, form, and consciousness—is contact;
and from that contact, feeling arises.
Craving has feeling as its condition, for one craves for the sake of feeling;
while craving, one grasps the fourfold grasping.
When there is grasping, existence proceeds for the grasper;
for if one were without grasping, one would be liberated and existence would not occur.
Those five aggregates are existence (bhava), and from existence, birth proceeds;
[from birth proceed] old age, death, suffering, and so forth, along with grief and lamentation.
Mental distress and despair proceed from birth;
thus occurs the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

Because the ignorant person constructs the formative forces (saṃskāra), which are the root of saṃsāra, the ignorant person is therefore the agent; the wise person is not, because of their vision of reality.
When ignorance has ceased, there is the non-arising of volitional formations;
the cessation of ignorance, however, results from the cultivation of this very knowledge.
Through the cessation of each respective [condition], that very [effect] does not proceed;
thus this entire mass of suffering is completely extinguished.
The views "I existed in past time" and "I did not exist" [arise from this].
Those [views] beginning with the eternity of the world which rely upon the prior limit;
The views such as "I shall not exist" and "shall I exist in a future time? are based upon the posterior limit [of existence].
"It was I in past time"—this is not tenable;
for he who existed in previous births is not this very same person.
If it were the case that "that very [appropriation] is the self," then appropriation would be distinguished [as the self].
But then, what indeed is your self apart from appropriation?
If it is maintained that there is no self apart from the appropriated aggregates,
then for you it would follow that the appropriated aggregates themselves are the self, yet [you still claim] that the self does not exist.
Nor is the appropriation itself the self, for that [appropriation] passes away and arises.
How indeed could the appropriation be the appropriator?
Furthermore, a self that is distinct from the appropriation is not tenable;
for if it were distinct, it would be perceived as being without appropriation, yet it is not so perceived.

Thus, the self is neither other than the appropriations nor is it the appropriation itself; there is no self that is without appropriation, yet it is not the case that it does not exist—this is the certainty.
"It was not the case that I existed in past time"—this is not tenable;
for this [present person] is not other than that [person] in previous births.
For if this [person] were other [than the aggregates], he would exist even after rejecting them;
likewise, he would remain there [independently] and would be born immortal.
The annihilation of actions, the destruction [of past deeds], and the fact that one person would experience the fruit of an action performed by another— such consequences as these would follow.
Nor has it arisen from non-existence, for in that case a fault would follow:
either the self would be something created, or it would have come into being without a cause.
Thus, regarding the past, the views that "I did not exist," "I existed," "both," or "neither"— none of these are tenable.
The view "Will I exist in the future time?
and "I will not exist" are the same as [the analysis] regarding the past time.
If that god were also that human being, then there would be permanence;
moreover, the god would be unarisen, for that which is permanent is not born.
If the human were other than the god, then there would be non-eternality;
if the human were other than the god, then continuity would not be possible.
If one part were divine and another part human, it would be both non-eternal and eternal; and that is not tenable.
If both the non-eternal and the eternal were established, then indeed the eternal would be established, as would the non-eternal. (MMK 27.18)
If someone had come from somewhere and were to go again to somewhere else, then cyclic existence would be beginningless; however, that is not the case.
If there exists nothing that is eternal, what could there be that is non-eternal? Or something both eternal and non-eternal, or one that is excluded from both of these?
If the world were finite, how could there be a future world?
Moreover, if the world were infinite, how could there be a future world?
Since this continuum of the aggregates is like the flame of a lamp,
it is therefore neither logical that it be infinite nor that it be finite.
If these aggregates were to be destroyed previously and yet these [present] aggregates were not to arise in dependence upon those [past] aggregates, then the world would be finite.
If these aggregates were not destroyed in the past, nor were they produced [in the future],
depending upon these aggregates, then the world would be infinite.
If one part were finite and another part were infinite, then the world would be both finite and infinite; and that is not tenable.
How, first of all, could one part of the appropriator perish while another part does not perish? This is not tenable.
And how indeed could one part of appropriation perish while another part does not perish? This too is not tenable.
If both the finite and the infinite were established as real,
then it would be established that [the world] is neither finite nor infinite, according to your wish.
Alternatively, since all entities are empty, where, for whom, which, and from what cause could views such as eternalism and so forth possibly arise?
I pay homage to Gautama, who, out of compassion, taught the true Dharma for the sake of abandoning all views.
